=== FILE: Delt Training at Long vs Short Muscle Lengths [_3RbWjzTFA8].en.txt ===

There's a ton of research that's been published lately showing that training a muscle at longer lengths is superior to training a muscle at shorter lengths in terms of hypertrophy. So, the evidence-based bros have taken this to mean that exercises working in a short position, like a hip thrust, suck and exercises that work in a long length position, like squats, are vastly superior. There is no research showing that squats are superior to hip thrusts for glute growth. They're basing these claims off of research pertaining to the biceps, the triceps, the calves, the quads, and the hamstrings. So, are the glutes unique? Do they respond better to short length position exercises? Or are there physiological principles governing all muscles and do all muscles respond better to training them at longer lengths? Time will tell. I want to show you why these guys don't know what the hell they're talking about. They will tell you that there's zero torque at the bottom of a hip thrust, but there is. In fact, the hip extension torque in a hip thrust is fairly consistent and it's high throughout the whole range of motion. You know what exercise does have zero torque in the bottom position in the lengthened position? Lateral raises and bent over rear delt raises. Laterals and bent over rear delts only work you in the shortened position. In the lengthened position, there's no torque. But, they're not going after these delt exercises. We have all these evidence-based bros going after a hip thrust while conveniently ignoring concentration curls, lateral raises, pec deck, and things of that nature. So, if they really believed in what they say that you should only perform exercises that work you in a lengthened position, then this is how you would do lateral raises. === FILE: Hip Thrust Moment Calculation [sdYrsk60wMw].en.txt ===

Hi guys, this is Andrew Vagotsski and Brit Contrera has asked me to film a short video explaining how to find the hip extension moment in the hip thrust. And it's not as simple as it seems because uh I'll start first uh with an example of the squat. So typically people think okay there's the barbell if you draw the force vector. Sorry about that. Um anyway, if you draw the force vector going down, which would be that line, then the moment arm to the hip would be that. The moment arm to the knee would be that. And while that's true, it ignores uh all of the body weight. Um so that's problematic. So a better way to look at it is if we look at the force vector coming up, but then it becomes less accurate as we go up. So, it's full of problems and it's not necessarily the most accurate, but it does allow for AI don't a good fast estimate as opposed to breaking down each segment individually and looking at the moments. So, we're going to use something that's based on that type of idea for the hip thrust. But how we're going to do it is a little bit different because the hip thrust is a much more complicated exercise and you'll see in why in a minute. If we have a load right here on top of the hips and the force vector from that load is going to go down. Now, one proposed way of looking at it is if we draw the hips over here, there's the femur, there's the torso, and there's the load. And it's not a perfect drawing, I know, but you get the point. Let's say the load is just off center from the hips. That would mean the moment arm is tiny. And that's what some people say. But if you look at how this load acts, this load would act to extend the hip, which means that your hip flexors would have to be used in order to flex the hip or resist that extension, which doesn't make sense. That means the load would do all the work going up. And for what the hip thrust is, that's that's not a good model. So we have to look at it another way. In the hip thrust, there are two points of contact. There's uh where the back touches the bench right here, and there's where the foot touches the floor. So, if we were to put a force plate right where the foot is, uh you're going to see a force vector coming out of the foot. Now, it won't just be vertical, but there will also be a horizontal force vector. And this is because your knees act or your hip extensors actively try to extend the knee which is going to try to basically force your shank that way. But because you're on the ground, it the ground is going to try to resist that and that's going to create a force vector that way. So you're then going to get a force vector that's like that that's somewhat diagonal. And because this won't account for all of your body's weight plus the load of that, there's also going to be a force vector coming out of the bench. And it's going to have to be equal and opposite. The horizontal is going to have to be equal and opposite to this. So you have that. And then the vertical is going to have to be the difference between uh the magnitude of this and the sum of the load plus the body weight. So we're going to have that coming up. So that's going to produce another force vector like that. Now, if we were to extend these force vectors out, bear with my terrible drawing, then you're going to have to draw the moment arms from the hip joint out to the position of the load vector or the ground reaction force. And also and these lines basically represent the moment arms which are the perpendicular distance from the line of action. So that would be the reaction force at the bench and the reaction force at the floor and those would be the moment arms. Then we would take so that's the moment arm from the bench and this is the force from the bench. Then we have the moment arm from the floor and then we have the force from the floor. So then in order to find the moment at the hip and we're going to do the absolute value of it, it's going to be equal to the force from the bench times the moment arm from the bench plus the force from the floor times the moment arm from the floor. And that's a very oversimplified way to look at how to find the hip extension moment and the hip thrust. It's kind of complicated, but basically, they divided the EMG activity by an inferior position, a bent- legged isometric hip extension test, rather than the gold standard, which is bent-leg hip extension in full hip extension against resistance applied to the manual thigh. If you put plates and bands on, then it's an even resistance curve, challenging the muscle throughout the entire range of motion. If you use all band resistance, it's easier in the lengthen position and then harder in the shortened position. So less in the stretch, more in the squeeze. So if you study hypertrophy science, this is a very hot topic right now. Many muscles benefit with regards to hypertrophy when they're trained in the lengthen position, but not all of them. And with the glutius maximus, it's currently up for debate. We've got two studies supporting a lengthen position and three studies showing that they seem to be equal. Now, the studies supporting the length of position involve Kubo 2019, and it showed that deeper squats grew significantly more glutes and adductors than shallow squats. And that makes sense. The deeper you go, the more you're going to use your hips. Now, there are some flaws with that study because the shallow squats could have just done a knee bend. They just looked at knee angle. They didn't look at hip angle. Nevertheless, that's one in favor of training the glutes at longer length. And then the second paper hasn't been published yet. This was conducted by Mao. So that's another in support of training the glutes at long lengths. The other three papers are Plotkin 2023. This one showed that squats tied hip thrust for glutius maximus growth. And if you think about squats stretch your glutes more and they're harder in the stretch, whereas hip thrusts involve less hip range of motion and they're harder in the squeeze position. So if long lengths and high torque at long lengths were all that, the squat would have greatly outperformed the hip thrust. But they tied. And the reason why this is important is because if you're okay with doing more volume, you can handle much more volume with hip thrust than you can squats. Squats beat up your body a lot more than hip thrust. All right, the next study is Cassiono 2024. And stiff legs, leg press, and hip thrust grew the glutes 9.3%. So, triple the glute growth. When you continue to add sets, it's not linear. You should see it tapering off. So, the fact that it's linear means that the hip thrust could be really good for glutes, potentially better than leg press and stiff legs. And then finally, we have the Bartholomew 2024 paper, and it showed that squats and step-ups tied hip thrust and reverse hypers for glutius maximus growth. So again, squats and step-ups involve more stretch and more torque at long lengths, whereas hip thrust and reverse hypers are more of a squeeze exercise and they challenge endrange hip extension more and they tied for glute growth.
